query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior can emerge not from impurity segregation or intermetallic precipitation but from a dynamic process in which high strain-rate deformation induces extreme grain refinement at high-angle grain boundaries. This refinement suppresses dislocation-mediated plasticity (i.e., an inverse Hall-Petch effect) and results in localized grain-boundary sliding that concentrates stress and promotes microvoid formation (cavitation) and decohesion, ultimately leading to brittle failure.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy (for example, CoCrFeMnNi) with a homogeneous microstructure and negligible boundary segregation.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled high strain-rate sliding (or shear) tests in an ultra-high vacuum or inert environment to suppress thermal segregation effects.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at various strain rates and temperatures (focusing on low to moderate temperatures where thermal diffusion is minimal) and under chemically inert (UHV) conditions to isolate the effects of dynamic grain refinement.
generation.structural_mediator: High-angle grain boundaries that, under high shear, dynamically refine to nanoscale dimensions and become sites for stress concentration and eventual decohesion.
generation.mechanism: The applied high strain rate promotes severe plastic deformation that reduces the effective grain size at the surface below a critical threshold. This inverse Hall-Petch behavior shifts the deformation mode from dislocation activity to grain-boundary sliding. The localized shear at these ultrafine grain boundaries leads to the nucleation and growth of microvoids (cavitation), which coalesce into cracks and cause brittle fracture, independent of any chemical segregation or precipitate formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial ductile baseline, the alloy will show a transition to brittle failure characterized by sudden fracture, evidence of microvoid coalescence and grain-boundary decohesion, and possibly reduced fracture toughness. This brittle behavior will be more pronounced under high strain-rate conditions without significant grain-boundary segregation.
generation.baseline: The alloy in its initial state exhibits favorable strength–ductility with ductile failure modes when deformed at lower strain rates or conditions that do not induce extreme grain refinement.
generation.boundary: The mechanistic transition is expected under service conditions where the applied strain rate is high and the operating temperature is low enough to prevent diffusional segregation, typically in environments free from chemically reactive species (e.g., UHV).
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical strain rate, grain-size threshold, and temperature range at which the transition from ductile to brittle behavior occurs remain to be precisely quantified and may depend on the alloy’s specific composition and processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare uniform samples of the single-phase HEA and perform sliding or shear tests under identical UHV conditions. Test a set at high strain rates intended to induce extreme grain refinement and compare to control samples tested under lower strain rates (or with a slight temperature increase to encourage segregation). Conduct in-situ microscopy (e.g., TEM/SEM) and evaluate fracture surfaces to assess grain-boundary structure, microvoid formation, and fracture mode.
measurements: Fracture toughness and mode (ductile vs brittle)
Grain size distribution at and near the surface using high-resolution microscopy
Direct observation of grain-boundary decohesion or cavitation features in the deformed zone
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high strain-rate tests in UHV do not show a transition to brittle failure (i.e., no evidence of pronounced grain boundary decohesion or cavitation) compared to low-strain-rate controls, or if brittle behavior is only observed in samples where segregation or intermetallic formation is induced, then the hypothesis of dynamic, strain-induced grain-boundary decohesion as the origin of brittle behavior is falsified.

In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions.
